explanations.answer: The people sinned and did not obey Him
explanations.explanation: That's the reason Nebuzaradan, Babylon's captain of the guard, gives. He says, "Because you people have sinned against the LORD and have not obeyed His voice, this thing has happened to you." He also says the LORD has done just as He said. Nobody in this passage is guessing at the cause, because the captain spells it out.

explanations.answer: The king of Judah broke his treaty
explanations.explanation: Nice try, friend, but a treaty never comes up in these verses. Nebuzaradan gives a different reason: "Because you people have sinned against the LORD and have not obeyed His voice, this thing has happened to you." He says the LORD decreed this disaster and fulfilled it, just as He said. So the reason on the table is sin and not obeying.

explanations.answer: Babylon simply had a bigger army
explanations.explanation: Armies are on the scene, I'll give you that. But the captain of the guard doesn't point to Babylon's strength at all. He says the LORD has done just as He said, "Because you people have sinned against the LORD and have not obeyed His voice, this thing has happened to you." That's the reason he gives.

I get why you'd think so, since the man holding the keys to the chains is a Babylonian captain. But the text says the opposite. Nebuzaradan tells Jeremiah, "If it pleases you to come with me to Babylon, then come…" and then, "But if it seems wrong to you to come with me to Babylon, go no farther." It's an offer, and Jeremiah gets to choose.

That's right. Nebuzaradan says, "If it pleases you to come with me to Babylon, then come, and I will take care of you." Then he adds, "But if it seems wrong to you to come with me to Babylon, go no farther." Nothing forces Jeremiah either way. The chains are off and the choice is his.

You've got it. Nebuzaradan says, "If it pleases you to come with me to Babylon, then come, and I will take care of you." That's the whole offer. No job title, no property, just that he'll look after Jeremiah.

That's a fancy title, but nobody offers Jeremiah a job in this passage. Nebuzaradan only says, "If it pleases you to come with me to Babylon, then come, and I will take care of you." Taking care of him is the promise. A desk with his name on it never comes up.

A field would be a nice housewarming gift, but it's not in the text. What Nebuzaradan says is, "If it pleases you to come with me to Babylon, then come, and I will take care of you." So the offer is simply that he'll take care of Jeremiah.

Yes. Nebuzaradan says Gedaliah is the one "whom the king of Babylon has appointed over the cities of Judah." Gedaliah got his post from the same king whose army took the city. That's how Nebuzaradan describes it.

Egypt is a good guess, since it was a big name in that part of the world. But the text says Gedaliah was appointed by "the king of Babylon." Nebuzaradan says it right there in verse 5, as he points Jeremiah toward Gedaliah.
Assyria is a real kingdom, but it's not the one in this verse. Nebuzaradan says Gedaliah was appointed over the cities of Judah by "the king of Babylon." That's the king behind the whole arrangement.

Right on the money. The text says, "Then the captain of the guard gave him a ration and a gift and released him." So Jeremiah leaves with food for the road and a present besides. That's a better send-off than most of us get from a job.
A letter would be handy for introductions, but the text doesn't mention one. It says the captain of the guard "gave him a ration and a gift and released him." The word you want is gift.

A guard sounds protective, but nobody gets assigned to Jeremiah here. The text says the captain of the guard "gave him a ration and a gift and released him." That word is gift, and then Jeremiah is free to go.

Close, but no. Nebuzaradan offered Babylon and said he would take care of Jeremiah. The text says, "So Jeremiah went to Gedaliah son of Ahikam at Mizpah and stayed with him among the people who were left in the land." Jeremiah stayed in the land.

That's right. Jeremiah went the other way: "So Jeremiah went to Gedaliah son of Ahikam at Mizpah and stayed with him among the people who were left in the land." Babylon was on the table, and he stayed put. I think that tells you plenty about where he wanted to be.
Yep. Verse 8 says they "came to Gedaliah at Mizpah," and they brought their men along. The commanders heard about Gedaliah and went to him. Mizpah is where Gedaliah is staying.

I can see why you'd hesitate, since these are army commanders and might do anything. But the text says it plainly: "they came to Gedaliah at Mizpah." They heard the king of Babylon had put him in charge, and they showed up with their men.

That's it. Gedaliah tells them, "Do not be afraid to serve the Chaldeans. Live in the land and serve the king of Babylon, and it will go well with you." The Chaldeans are the Babylonians. He swore an oath to say it.

The Ammonites do come up later in this passage, but not here. In his oath, Gedaliah says, "Do not be afraid to serve the Chaldeans." The Chaldeans are the Babylonians, and that's what he tells them not to fear.

Gedaliah says nothing about going to Jerusalem. His oath is, "Do not be afraid to serve the Chaldeans. Live in the land and serve the king of Babylon, and it will go well with you." The Chaldeans are the Babylonians, so serving them is the thing he says not to fear.

Correct. Gedaliah says, "As for me, I will stay in Mizpah to represent you before the Chaldeans who come to us." So when the Babylonians come around, he's the one who speaks for them. That's his job at Mizpah.

Walls would be a big project, but Gedaliah never mentions them. He says, "As for me, I will stay in Mizpah to represent you before the Chaldeans who come to us." His job is to speak for the people when the Babylonians arrive.

explanations.answer: Train them for the next battle
explanations.explanation: Gedaliah's plan is much calmer than that. He says, "As for me, I will stay in Mizpah to represent you before the Chaldeans who come to us." He'll speak for them to the Babylonians, and he tells the men to gather their harvest.

That's right. The text says "they all returned from all the places to which they had been banished and came to the land of Judah, to Gedaliah at Mizpah." They had heard the king of Babylon left a remnant and appointed Gedaliah. So they came home.

Staying put would be the easy move, but that's not what happens. The text says "they all returned from all the places to which they had been banished and came to the land of Judah, to Gedaliah at Mizpah." Once they heard the news, they headed home.

No gifts are mentioned in these verses. What the text says is that "they all returned from all the places to which they had been banished and came to the land of Judah, to Gedaliah at Mizpah." They came back themselves.

Yes. Johanan, son of Kareah and one of the army commanders, and the others ask Gedaliah, "Are you aware that Baalis king of the Ammonites has sent Ishmael son of Nethaniah to take your life?" Taking his life means killing him. That's the warning.

Spying would be sneaky enough, but it's not what the commanders say. Their warning is that Baalis king of the Ammonites "has sent Ishmael son of Nethaniah to take your life." The word you want is kill, and it's a much bigger deal than spying.

Robbery is bad, but the warning is far heavier than that. The commanders ask, "Are you aware that Baalis king of the Ammonites has sent Ishmael son of Nethaniah to take your life?" They're talking about killing Gedaliah.

I see why you'd think so, since the warning came from his own commanders. But the text says, "But Gedaliah son of Ahikam did not believe them." He heard that Ishmael had been sent to take his life, and he didn't buy it.
That's right. The text says it straight: "But Gedaliah son of Ahikam did not believe them." The commanders told him Ishmael had been sent to take his life, and Gedaliah didn't believe it.
Yes. Johanan says, "Let me go and kill Ishmael son of Nethaniah." He adds, "No one will know it." That's his offer, and he makes it privately.
A bodyguard plan would be a lot gentler. But Johanan's offer is different: "Let me go and kill Ishmael son of Nethaniah." He says it quietly, and adds, "No one will know it."
Shipping Ishmael off isn't in the plan. Johanan says, "Let me go and kill Ishmael son of Nethaniah," and then adds, "No one will know it." It's a much more serious offer than a trip.

That's the word. Johanan asks, "Why should he take your life and scatter all the people of Judah who have gathered to you, so that the remnant of Judah would perish?" The remnant is the people who are left. He's saying the stakes reach well beyond Gedaliah.

That would be the happy ending, but it's the opposite of what Johanan says. He asks, "Why should he take your life and scatter all the people of Judah who have gathered to you, so that the remnant of Judah would perish?" He's worried about the remnant perishing.

Rebelling isn't what Johanan is worried about. He asks, "Why should he take your life and scatter all the people of Judah who have gathered to you, so that the remnant of Judah would perish?" The word is perish.
Yes. Gedaliah answers Johanan with, "Do not do such a thing!" Then he says, "What you are saying about Ishmael is a lie." So he turns down the offer and calls the claim a lie.

Gedaliah does say it. The text has him answer Johanan, "Do not do such a thing! What you are saying about Ishmael is a lie." Johanan offered to deal with Ishmael, and Gedaliah shut the idea down right away.
